summary:
Jambi is a province of Indonesia, and the national framework applies there in full: Indonesia's penal code, national morality provisions, document rules and policing practice govern a visitor in Jambi as they govern anyone else in the country. No Jambi-specific ordinance, protection measure or documented incident against a transgender person was found in the sources reviewed.

The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic. A separate source records a maximum of one year, on complaint by an immediate family member.

Same-sex conduct is otherwise not criminalised in private under national law. Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, and two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship there in February 2025. Provincial moral laws of this kind remain part of the enforcement texture across Indonesia.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs attacked transgender people across Indonesia in a wave of 14 to 16 July 2026, including more than 15 trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage shared online. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge directly to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 issued by President Prabowo Subianto, which lists LGBTQ+ people and "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among nonmilitary threats to be monitored and controlled alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy. On 11 August 2025 three men were arrested over an LGBTQ community page on Facebook.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.
tangentialFactors:
Public hostility is documented at national scale. A 2025 Pew survey found that 93% of Indonesians regard homosexuality as morally unacceptable, and a researcher cited in August 2026 reporting documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016.

Indonesia's diplomatic position tracks the same direction: the country voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

Jambi sits inside a patchwork rather than a uniform regime. Two provinces criminalise same-sex conduct under provincial religious law while Jambi has no such ordinance on record, so the practical exposure of a visitor changes at provincial borders, most sharply in Aceh.

Partner recognition is unavailable: same-sex marriage is not permitted anywhere in Indonesia, so a visitor's relationship carries no legal standing and the extra-marital sex provision has no marital exemption to fall back on.

The extra-marital sex provision can be set in motion by a complaint from an immediate family member, which places consensual same-sex conduct inside the reach of household disputes as well as policing.

outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty under the 2022 penal code is recorded inconsistently across sources, two years in one and one year on complaint by an immediate family member in another; the discrepancy is unresolved here and the operative figure should be confirmed against the statute text.

No Jambi-specific ordinance, protection measure or documented incident against a transgender person was found in the sources reviewed. Whether Jambi has enacted provincial religious bylaws with effect on visitors, and whether any have been enforced, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Enforcement frequency of the extra-marital sex provision since it took effect on 2 January 2026 is not sourced for Jambi or nationally beyond the reporting that prosecutions are selective.

The status and fate of the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour is unresolved; it was under discussion and no outcome is recorded here.

Whether Jambi police have conducted raids on LGBT gatherings, as officers did in the Puncak area in June 2025, is not sourced.
